content: Abacavir is a nucleoside analogue approved by the FDA for the treatment of HIV-1 infection. It is marketed under the brand name Ziagen and is available in tablet and oral solution forms. The tablets contain 300 mg of abacavir sulfate, while the oral solution contains 20 mg/mL of abacavir sulfate. The oral solution is a clear to opalescent, yellowish liquid with a strawberry-banana flavor. Black Box Warning Abacavir carries a Black Box Warning due to the risk of serious and potentially fatal hypersensitivity reactions. Patients with the HLA-B5701 allele are at a significantly higher risk of developing such reactions. Screening for the HLA-B5701 allele is recommended before initiating or reinitiating abacavir therapy. If a hypersensitivity reaction is suspected, abacavir must be discontinued immediately and permanently. Reintroduction of abacavir after a hypersensitivity reaction can result in more severe symptoms, including life-threatening hypotension and death. Adult Indications and Dosage Abacavir is indicated for use in combination with other antiretroviral agents for the treatment of HIV-1 infection. The recommended oral dose for adults is 600 mg daily, which can be administered as 300 mg twice daily or 600 mg once daily. For patients with mild hepatic impairment (Child-Pugh score 5-6), the recommended dose is 200 mg twice daily, and the oral solution should be used to enable dose reduction. Abacavir is contraindicated in patients with moderate to severe hepatic impairment. Pediatric Indications and Dosage For pediatric patients aged 3 months and older, the recommended oral dose of the solution is 8 mg/kg twice daily, up to a maximum of 300 mg twice daily, in combination with other antiretroviral agents. Pediatric patients weighing 14 kg or more may use the tablet form if they can reliably swallow tablets. If not, the oral solution should be prescribed. Contraindications Abacavir is contraindicated in patients with a history of hypersensitivity to abacavir or any of its components. It is also contraindicated in patients with moderate or severe hepatic impairment. Abacavir should never be restarted in patients who have experienced a hypersensitivity reaction, regardless of their HLA-B5701 status. Hypersensitivity Reactions Hypersensitivity to abacavir is a multi-organ clinical syndrome that typically involves symptoms from at least two of the following groups: fever, rash, gastrointestinal symptoms (nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, or abdominal pain), respiratory symptoms (dyspnea, cough, or pharyngitis), and constitutional symptoms (malaise, fatigue, or achiness). Symptoms usually appear within the first six weeks of treatment, with a median onset of nine days. Laboratory abnormalities associated with hypersensitivity may include elevated liver function tests, elevated creatine phosphokinase, elevated creatinine, and lymphopenia. If hypersensitivity is suspected, abacavir must be discontinued immediately and permanently. Lactic Acidosis and Severe Hepatomegaly with Steatosis Lactic acidosis and severe hepatomegaly with steatosis, including fatal cases, have been reported with the use of nucleoside analogues, including abacavir. These events are more common in women and patients with prolonged nucleoside exposure. Treatment with abacavir should be suspended in any patient who develops clinical or laboratory findings suggestive of lactic acidosis or pronounced hepatotoxicity. Immune Reconstitution Syndrome Immune reconstitution syndrome has been reported in patients treated with combination antiretroviral therapy, including abacavir. During the initial phase of treatment, patients may develop an inflammatory response to residual opportunistic infections, necessitating further evaluation and treatment. Autoimmune disorders, such as Graves’ disease and Guillain-Barré syndrome, have also been reported in the context of immune reconstitution, with variable onset times. Fat Redistribution Redistribution or accumulation of body fat, including central obesity, dorsocervical fat enlargement (buffalo hump), peripheral wasting, facial wasting, and breast enlargement, has been observed in patients receiving antiretroviral therapy. The mechanism and long-term consequences of these events are not fully understood. Adverse Reactions The most significant adverse reactions associated with abacavir include hypersensitivity reactions, lactic acidosis, severe hepatomegaly, immune reconstitution syndrome, and fat redistribution. In clinical trials, hypersensitivity reactions occurred in approximately 8% of patients. Once-daily dosing of abacavir has been associated with a higher incidence of severe hypersensitivity reactions compared to twice-daily dosing. Drug Interactions Abacavir does not affect the pharmacokinetics of ethanol, but ethanol decreases the elimination of abacavir, leading to increased overall exposure. Methadone has no clinically significant effect on abacavir pharmacokinetics, but methadone clearance may increase, potentially requiring dose adjustments in some patients. Use in Specific Populations Pregnancy: Abacavir is classified as Pregnancy Category C. Animal studies have shown fetal malformations and developmental toxicity at high doses. Abacavir should be used during pregnancy only if the potential benefits outweigh the risks. An Antiretroviral Pregnancy Registry has been established to monitor outcomes in pregnant women exposed to abacavir. Nursing Mothers: HIV-infected mothers are advised not to breastfeed to prevent postnatal transmission of HIV-1. It is unknown if abacavir is excreted in human milk, but it is secreted into the milk of lactating rats. Pediatric Use: The safety and effectiveness of abacavir have been established in pediatric patients aged 3 months to 13 years. Geriatric Use: Clinical studies did not include sufficient numbers of patients aged 65 and older to determine whether they respond differently from younger patients. Dose selection for elderly patients should be cautious, reflecting the greater frequency of decreased hepatic, renal, or cardiac function. Renal and Hepatic Impairment: Abacavir is contraindicated in patients with moderate to severe hepatic impairment. There is no FDA guidance on its use in patients with renal impairment. Overdosage There is no known antidote for abacavir overdose. It is not known whether abacavir can be removed by peritoneal dialysis or hemodialysis. Mechanism of Action Abacavir is a synthetic nucleoside analogue that is converted by cellular enzymes to its active metabolite, carbovir triphosphate (CBV-TP). CBV-TP inhibits HIV-1 reverse transcriptase by competing with the natural substrate deoxyguanosine-5′-triphosphate (dGTP) and by incorporating into viral DNA, leading to chain termination. CBV-TP is a weak inhibitor of cellular DNA polymerases α, β, and γ. Structural Information Abacavir sulfate is a white to off-white solid with a solubility of approximately 77 mg/mL in distilled water at 25°C. Each tablet contains abacavir sulfate equivalent to 300 mg of abacavir as the active ingredient, along with inactive ingredients such as colloidal silicon dioxide and magnesium stearate.
